newsitem.title: UK: N. Ireland's Sinn Fein attacks Bruton's "mistakes".
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland's Sinn Fein attacks Bruton's "mistakes".

text.p: The IRA's Sinn Fein political arm on Sunday accused Irish Prime Minister John Bruton of ineptitude which it said had helped wreck Northern Irish peace moves.

In scathing terms, highlighting a gulf with Bruton nine months into an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombing campaign, Sinn Fein said Britain's refusal to bring it into talks during a 17-month truce caused the ceasefire's collapse in February.

"It has to be said that at critical junctures Mr Bruton made serious mistakes and misjudgments which contributed to the breakdown of the peace process," Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin said in County Cork in southwest Ireland.

He cited Bruton's refusal to meet Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams and moderate nationalist leader John Hume to discuss a peace process impasse last October and his support for IRA arms decommissioning, which Sinn Fein said bogged down the process for months.
McLaughlin attacked Bruton's "failure to represent or even to comprehend the plight of small nationalist communities" during a tense summer of parades by pro-British Orangemen.

McLaughlin's comments, some of the harshest by Sinn Fein about Bruton, followed the Irish leader's criticism of the so-called Republican Movement, comprising Sinn Fein and the IRA, after guerrilla bombs killed a British soldier near Belfast two weeks ago.
McLaughlin said that he was replying as national chairman of Sinn Fein to "political and personal insults" which Bruton had directed at his party's leadership over the past 10 days.

"The Taoiseach's (prime minister's) willingness to retreat into the old and failed agenda of vilification can only raise further questions about the depth of his commitment to this (peace) project since he came to office."

Bruton united with his British counterpart, John Major, in condemning the IRA's October 7 attack. It was its first in Northern Ireland for more than two years and marked the extension of a bombing wave that had been mainly confined to mainland Britain.
Reflecting widespread Irish revulsion, Bruton described it as a cynical betrayal of the Northen Irish peace process.
The strategy of "the ballot box in one hand and the gun in the other" was first originated by the Nazis in Germany before World War Two, he declared.
If the Republican movement wanted to be taken seriously as democrats they would have to get rid of the tactical use of violence forever, he said.
Britain and Ireland have excluded Sinn Fein from multi-party talks held in Belfast since June, saying the IRA must first end its war against British rule.
